title: How Personalized Medicine Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain personalized medicine, the idea that treatment should be matched to an individual's biology and genetics rather than to what works for most people. They trace its history from Hippocrates and early blood-type matching, through a World War II antimalarial anemia case, to the Human Genome Project. They cover pharmacogenetics, adverse drug events, falling genome sequencing costs (compared to Moore's law), and examples such as the cystic fibrosis drug Kalydeco, the breast cancer drug Herceptin, and an artificial pancreas and tinnitus devices for diabetes and hearing. Obstacles discussed include cost, data processing, the Angelina Jolie effect and overtesting, FDA capacity, genetic discrimination laws (GINA), and the 23andMe database and its deal with Genentech. The episode ends with listener mail about satanic panic movies.

segments.title: Opening and tour promo
segments.summary: Hosts promote live tour dates and the SYSK Live site, then open with banter about personalized medicine.

segments.title: History of individualized medicine
segments.summary: Hippocrates' idea that knowing the person matters more than knowing the disease; trial and error in Western medicine; Landsteiner and Hektoen's blood type matching; family histories; the World War II antimalarial anemia case among African American troops and its G6PD-related cause.

segments.title: Human Genome Project and pharmacogenetics
segments.summary: The Human Genome Project changed the field by linking genes and molecular pathways to disease and drug response. Pharmacogenetics matches drugs to a patient's genome, and adverse drug events are cited as a motivation, with about 770,000 US injuries or deaths a year.

segments.title: Falling genome sequencing costs and future devices
segments.summary: Sequencing cost fell from about a million dollars for James Watson's 2007 genome to under two dollars for sequencing and roughly fifteen thousand dollars for full analysis. Raymond McCauley's Moore's law comparison is noted, computing power for analysis is the bottleneck, and the hosts speculate about toilet-based urine sequencers, wearables, and phone apps tied to health records.

segments.title: Examples: cystic fibrosis, Herceptin, diabetes and hearing devices
segments.summary: Kalydeco was approved in 2012 for the roughly four percent of cystic fibrosis patients with a specific genetic mutation, changing understanding of the disease. Herceptin targets breast tumors expressing a specific protein. A wearable artificial pancreas for type 1 diabetes was entering clinical trials, and customizable hearing or tinnitus devices were mentioned.

segments.title: Obstacles: cost, the Angelina Jolie effect, FDA and genetic discrimination
segments.summary: Obstacles include cost, data processing, and overstating findings; the Angelina Jolie effect of preventive surgery and bioethicists' concern about health obsession. The FDA is overtaxed, a de-anonymization problem closed a public genome database, and biological discrimination was addressed by GINA, which passed with a near-unanimous vote, with Ron Paul the lone no in the House. Canada is noted as the only G7 country without such protection.

segments.title: 23andMe database and data privacy
segments.summary: 23andMe sold a $99 test, built a database of several hundred thousand customers' genomes, and made money from research deals, including a reported $60 million deal with Genentech to analyze Parkinson's genomes. Concerns about private genome databases are compared to Facebook data mining.

segments.title: Closing discussion and related episodes
segments.summary: Hosts suggest revisiting personalized medicine periodically and recommend related episodes on limb regrowth, grandparents' diet, blood, and computers replacing doctors.

segments.title: Listener mail: Satanic panic movies
segments.summary: A listener shares a top ten list of eighties movies with satanic themes and comments on the earlier Satanic Panic episode.
